What BMI can and cannot tell you

BMI is quick to calculate and widely used, which is why it is easy to over-read. Here is what it measures and where it falls short.

Educational estimates only. Results are not medical advice, a diagnosis, or a treatment plan. Talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your health. Read the full medical disclaimer.

How BMI is calculated

BMI is your weight in kilograms divided by your height in metres, squared. For adults, the CDC and WHO describe four screening categories: below 18.5 (underweight), 18.5 to 24.9 (healthy weight), 25 to 29.9 (overweight) and 30 or above (obesity). You can work it out with the adult BMI calculator.

What it is good for

Because it needs only height and weight, BMI is a cheap, consistent way to screen groups of people. The CDC calls it a screening measure that should be considered alongside other factors, not a diagnosis.

What it cannot see

BMI does not measure body fat. It cannot tell muscle from fat, so a very muscular person can have a high BMI with little excess fat. It also says nothing about where fat is carried. NICE guidance notes that someone in the healthy BMI range may still carry too much fat around the middle, which is why it recommends a waist measurement too. You can try that with the waist-to-height ratio calculator.

Age and background matter

The CDC applies adult categories from age 20; for younger people it uses BMI-for-age charts, as does WHO for children. This website is for adults only. NICE also advises lower BMI thresholds for some ethnic groups when assessing health risk, so a single set of cut-offs is not the full picture.

A sensible way to use your result

Treat BMI as one data point. If you are curious about the weights that correspond to the healthy band for your height, the healthy weight range calculator shows them, with the same caveats. If a result worries you, or you have a health condition, talk to a doctor or other qualified professional rather than relying on a number from a website.
